I couldn’t find any HVAC booking in the system for that phone number in the October 10–20, 2025 window, so I don’t have a record I can directly submit a refund request on.

Given the timing, there’s another big constraint: a service done around October 15, 2025 is now far outside a normal refund period. Most policies only allow refunds for a limited time (often around 30 days from the service date, sometimes 60), so a direct refund at this point is very unlikely under standard terms, even if I had the booking record.

That said, you still have some realistic ways to push for a remedy:

1) Push for a proper fix (no-charge follow-up)  
- Grab any invoice, email, or work order from that visit and look for words like “guarantee,” “warranty,” “30‑day callback,” or “we stand behind our work.”  
- When you contact them, be very specific:
  - They serviced your system around October 15, 2025 to fix a heating issue.
  - The same problem came back within a few days and never really went away.
  - You’re asking for a no‑charge follow‑up visit to properly fix what was supposed to have been fixed the first time.

2) Ask for partial consideration if they resist  
- If they refuse to come out for free, ask for:
  - A heavily discounted follow‑up visit; or  
  - Partial store credit toward future work.  
That’s often easier for them to agree to than a full refund this long after the job.

3) Escalate if needed  
- Ask to speak with a manager or owner and calmly lay out:
  - What they were hired to fix;
  - That the same issue quickly returned;
  - That you effectively did not receive the benefit of what you paid for.
- If they’re a licensed HVAC contractor, you can also:
  - File a complaint with the state licensing or contractor’s board; and
  - Leave a detailed, factual review (dates, issue, and how they responded), which sometimes prompts them to make it right.

If you can paste the text from any invoice or confirmation email (especially anything describing what they repaired and any warranty/guarantee wording), I can:
- Tell you how strong your argument is under that specific wording, and
- Draft a short, firm email or phone script you can use to request either a no‑charge revisit or some form of credit/compensation.</action>
